discovery: Discovery of metal-halide perovskites as efficient photovoltaic absorbers and the invention of the solid-state perovskite solar cell
subfield: Condensed matter and materials physics / photovoltaics
motivation: In 2009 Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in a photovoltaic cell. In 2012 Park and, independently, Snaith with Miyasaka turned this into stable solid-state devices, and Snaith showed that the perovskite itself transports charge over long distances, so it can work as a thin-film absorber in planar cells. That was the step from a dye-cell variant to a new class of semiconductor. Perovskite cells are solution-processed at low temperature, yet they combine sharp absorption edges, long carrier diffusion lengths and unusual tolerance of defects. Their efficiency went from about 4% to over 26% in a decade, and perovskite–silicon tandems now exceed 33%. The physics of these soft, ionic semiconductors has opened a new research field, and the technology is close to commercial use, promising cheaper solar electricity. This discovery is of great use to humanity in the full sense of Nobel's will.
